clue.text: Divorce, beheaded, died, or lived it up

indicators.note: a beheaded word has lost its head, so the following word drops its opening letter

parts.note: to part is to separate, as a couple do in divorce
the word without its first letter

explanation.surface: A nod to the rhyme about Henry VIII's six wives: divorced, beheaded, died — or, in this version, partied.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface borrows the mnemonic 'divorced, beheaded, died, divorced, beheaded, survived' for Henry VIII's wives; 'beheaded' is no longer a fate but an instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: To party is to celebrate with gusto, so having partied is having lived it up.

clue.text: Rising out of bed, old woman's a cougar

indicators.note: in a down answer rising means reading from bottom to top, so the letters come out backwards

parts.note: someone out of bed is up
ma is a familiar word for mother, the old woman

explanation.surface: Getting up in the morning, an older woman turns out to be a cougar, slang for a woman who dates younger men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cougar' looks like the slang for an older woman chasing younger men, which the 'old woman' supports; here it is the big cat.
explanation.definitionFit: The puma, also called the cougar or mountain lion, is a large wild cat of the Americas.

clue.text: Making a comeback, Alexander Armstrong wraps special

indicators.note: making a comeback means returning, so the concealed letters are read in the opposite direction
something that wraps another holds it inside, so the letters sit within the name

parts.note: the letters straddling the end of the first name and the start of the surname

explanation.surface: TV presenter Alexander Armstrong, back on screen, wraps up a special episode.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Armstrong is a British comedian and host of the quiz show Pointless; his name only carries the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare and special both describe something uncommon and valued, so they are synonyms here.

clue.text: Cool part of an old-fashioned kitchen crumble, taking seconds

indicators.note: taking every second one means keeping the even-numbered letters and skipping the rest

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth letters and so on of these two words

explanation.surface: A cosy kitchen crumble from yesteryear, so good everyone takes second helpings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old-fashioned' looks like it describes the kitchen, but it is the Old Fashioned, a whisky cocktail served over ice; 'seconds' are not second helpings but every second letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An Old Fashioned cocktail is served on the rocks, so the frozen block of water is the chilling component of the drink.

clue.text: Cracking doctor's surgery is in decline

indicators.note: cracking something open lets another thing in, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: DR is the abbreviation for doctor, with the 's attached
an op is a surgical operation

explanation.surface: A doctor's practice that was once excellent is now going downhill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' reads as British praise (excellent) and 'surgery' as a GP's practice; both are doing other jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that drops falls or declines, so the verb in the third person matches 'is in decline'.

clue.text: Controversial Italian banker joins mile high clubs

indicators.note: someone high is intoxicated and in no fit state, so the word beside it is scrambled

parts.note: a river is a banker in crosswords because it has banks; the Po is Italy's longest
the four letters rearranged
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games

explanation.surface: A racy Italian banker, presumably the financier kind, joins the mile high club of in-flight lovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian banker' suggests a financier; it is the river Po. The 'mile high club' is slang for people who have had sex aboard a plane.
explanation.definitionFit: Polemic is used as an adjective for argumentative, disputatious writing or speech, which is controversial by design.

clue.text: Piano notes before special red carpet affairs

parts.note: P is the musical marking for piano, softly
re and mi are notes of the sol-fa scale
ere is an old word for before
S is an abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A pianist plays a few notes ahead of a special glitzy event.
explanation.definitionFit: Film premieres are first showings where stars walk a red carpet for the cameras.

clue.text: Some moving through Berlin in G-strings and extra layers

indicators.note: some of a run of words, travelling across them, means a section is taken from inside that stretch

parts.note: letters running from the end of the city across the next two words

explanation.surface: A few dancers move through a Berlin club wearing G-strings and extra layers.
explanation.definitionFit: Linings are inner layers sewn into garments, curtains and so on, beyond the main fabric.

clue.text: Rotate in order to find n

definitions.text: Rotate in order to find n

parts.words: Rotate in order to find n
parts.note: surface reading: a maths instruction to turn something to find an unknown value n
setter's reading: the lower-case letter n is what you get by turning the letter u upside down

explanation.surface: A puzzle instruction: rotate something to work out the value of n.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn a lower-case u through 180 degrees and it becomes an n, so turning the letter literally produces the reversal manoeuvre.
explanation.definitionFit: Making this manoeuvre in a vehicle means turning right round to head the opposite way, which is rotating.

clue.text: Condition of white cliffs leaves family drilling less

parts.note: cha is tea, made from leaves

indicators.note: drilling bores into something, so one piece is pushed inside the other

parts.note: taken as written
kin are one's family

explanation.surface: The state of the white cliffs means less drilling is permitted, and a family moves out.
explanation.walkthrough: Cha is slang for tea, hence 'leaves'. The white cliffs evoke those of Dover, on England's south coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The White Cliffs of Dover are made of chalk, so their characteristic quality is the property of being chalky.

clue.text: Where head of state is …?

parts.note: surface reading: a question about where a country's leader is, trailing off unfinished
setter's reading: the head of the word state is its first letter, and the ellipsis shows three dots, which is how that letter is sent in a signalling system of dots and dashes

explanation.surface: Someone asks where the head of state has got to and trails off into silence.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis is not hesitation but the content: S, the head of 'state', is three dots in Morse, so the clue asks where S is written '...'.
explanation.definitionFit: In the telegraph signalling system of dots and dashes, the letter S is represented as three short dots.

clue.text: Tech giant rolling back AI after new fine

indicators.note: after places the turned piece behind the words that follow it, so new and fine come first

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for new
OK means fine, all right

indicators.note: rolling back means going backwards, so the letters of AI are taken in the opposite direction

parts.note: taken as written, then turned around

explanation.surface: A tech giant retreats from artificial intelligence after a new fine from regulators.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fine' reads as a regulator's penalty, but it is OK, as in all right.
explanation.definitionFit: Nokia is the Finnish telecoms company, once the world's largest maker of mobile phones.

clue.text: Hunt one playing victim, showing sign of uncertainty

parts.note: a quest is a hunt or search
the Roman numeral for one
a show that is on is playing
a mark is a con artist's victim

explanation.surface: Someone hunts while pretending to be the victim, and their unease shows.
explanation.definitionFit: The ? punctuation mark signals a question, or more loosely doubt about something.

clue.text: Where a surfer stands straight?

definitions.meaning: first meaning, read literally: on top of the surfboard
second meaning: honest, open, with nothing hidden

explanation.surface: A question about how a surfer keeps upright on the waves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Straight' looks like upright posture, but it means honest; the question mark flags the literal reading of an idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means legitimate and honest, originally from card players keeping hands visible over the table.

clue.text: One masters a cryptic clue, catching a bit of trickery that's neat

indicators.note: catching something takes it into one's grip, so one group is placed inside the other

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: cryptic means puzzling, mysterious, so the word it qualifies appears in jumbled form

parts.note: M is an abbreviation for master, doubled for the plural
the article and the four-letter word rearranged together
the article taken as written

indicators.note: a bit is just a small piece, here the opening letter of the next word

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A solver who masters a cryptic clue, spotting its bit of trickery, finds it neat.
explanation.walkthrough: The scrambled 'a clue' wraps A plus T, the first letter of trickery, before its final E.
explanation.definitionFit: Immaculate means spotless and perfectly tidy, which is what neat means applied to a room or appearance.

clue.text: Electric vehicle behind a 50% reduction in carbon

indicators.note: cutting something by half keeps only one of its halves, so the next word loses its second half

parts.note: the bum is the behind, the buttocks
a, as in 'five pounds a head', means per
the first half of the word

explanation.surface: An electric car's selling point: a 50 per cent reduction in carbon emissions.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all about green motoring, but the electric vehicle is a fairground dodgem. 'A' for per is the 'a head' sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Fairground bumper cars, or dodgems, are small cars powered through a pole touching an electrified ceiling grid.

clue.text: Childish type in moccasins, for a change

indicators.note: making a change means altering the arrangement, so the preceding letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: An immature sort of person wearing moccasins for once.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Type' looks like a kind of person; it is typeface.
explanation.definitionFit: Comic Sans is a typeface modelled on comic-book lettering, often mocked as juvenile in appearance.

clue.text: One tempting polar resident to move north

indicators.note: north is the letter N, and telling it to move means that letter shifts to a new place in the word

parts.note: Father Christmas lives at the North Pole

explanation.surface: Someone tries to lure a polar bear or other Arctic dweller to relocate further north.
explanation.walkthrough: Only one letter moves: the N in the middle of SANTA goes to the end, turning Father Christmas into the Devil.
explanation.definitionFit: Satan is the tempter in Christian tradition, the Devil who tempted Christ in the wilderness.

clue.text: Using last drops of original Guinness bottles

parts.note: via means by way of, using

indicators.note: the last drops are what is left at the very end, so only the final letters of the following words count

parts.note: the final letter of each of these two words

explanation.surface: Someone drains the last drops of genuine Guinness from the bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'last drops of' looks like part of the drinking scene, but it picks out the end letters of 'original' and 'Guinness'.
explanation.definitionFit: Vials are small glass bottles, usually for medicine or perfume.

clue.text: Conceal undercover agent that's been discovered twice

parts.note: an undercover operation is secret

indicators.note: discovered here means uncovered, losing its outside, and doing it twice strips away two layers of outer letters

parts.note: strip the outer letters, then strip them again, leaving the centre

explanation.surface: A spy hides after their cover has been blown not once but twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Undercover agent' looks like one phrase for a spy, but splits in two; 'discovered' means losing a cover, applied twice to five letters.
explanation.definitionFit: To secrete something is to hide it away, a less common verb sense alongside the biological one of discharge.

clue.text: Butchers service lots of land

parts.note: Mass is a church service
acres are units of land area, and lots of land is measured in them

explanation.surface: A butcher's shop serves customers across a wide area of countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Butchers' looks like a noun for the tradespeople, but it is the verb: slaughters.
explanation.definitionFit: To butcher people is to slaughter them brutally, which is what one who massacres does.

clue.text: I regret raising a complaint

indicators.note: raising lifts one letter higher, which in a down answer moves it earlier, so the arrangement changes

parts.note: taken as written
to lament is to regret or mourn

explanation.surface: Someone apologises for having brought up a grievance.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'a' in the clue is not filler: it names the letter A in I LAMENT, which is raised to the top of the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A complaint in the medical sense is an illness or disorder, which is what an ailment is.

clue.text: Keep risking one's balance as a result of inflation

definitions.text: Keep risking one's balance as a result of inflation

parts.words: Keep risking one's balance as a result of inflation
parts.note: surface reading: someone repeatedly gambling their bank balance away because rising prices are biting
setter's reading: a keep is a castle's stronghold tower, and this one is unsteady underfoot because it has been blown up with air

explanation.surface: Rising prices force someone to keep gambling with their bank balance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' reads as a verb (continue) and 'balance' as money; really a keep is a fortress, the balance is physical, and the inflation is of air.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable children's play structure shaped like a fortress, on which jumping children struggle to stay upright.

clue.text: Utter chaos!

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as 'total chaos!', with 'Utter' an adjective; it is really a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means to declare; as a noun it is used for a disordered or agitated condition.

clue.text: Sunak on the offensive ultimately gets support for proposal

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letters of the preceding words are taken

parts.note: the final letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: Former Prime Minister Rishi Sunak goes on the attack and eventually wins backing for his plan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Proposal' suggests a political policy, but it is a marriage proposal, traditionally made down on one knee.
explanation.definitionFit: A suitor traditionally kneels to propose marriage, so the bent leg joint supports the proposer.

clue.text: Can king returning create cohesion?

indicators.note: in a down answer returning means going back up, so the pieces are read in reverse

parts.note: a tin is a can
K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A question of whether a returning monarch is able to unite the country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can' looks like the verb (is able to); it is the noun, a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: To knit is to join closely together, as broken bones knit or a team knits into a unit.

clue.text: Torquemada's last puzzle — wow!

indicators.note: the last of something is its end, so only the final letter of the name counts

parts.note: the final letter of the name
a maze is a puzzle of paths

explanation.surface: An admiring cry at the final puzzle by Torquemada, the famous early Observer crossword setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Torquemada was the pseudonym of Edward Powys Mathers, a celebrated Observer crossword setter of the 1920s and 30s, named after the Spanish Inquisitor.
explanation.definitionFit: To wow an audience is to astonish or impress them, a verb synonym.

clue.text: Old war hero is a criminal among men

indicators.note: something criminal is crooked or bent out of true, so the letters that follow are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, as fodder

explanation.surface: A veteran of a long-ago war turns out to be a crook living among ordinary men.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the article 'a' plus 'among men', nine letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Agamemnon, king of Mycenae, led the Greek forces in the Trojan War.

clue.text: In studies, returning leak gets trickier to plumb

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another, here the second item goes within the first

parts.note: a den is a private study or workroom

indicators.note: returning means going back the way it came, so the word for leak is read backwards

parts.note: to take a leak is to urinate, have a pee

explanation.surface: A plumber finds a recurring leak in the study harder and harder to fix.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plumb' teases plumbing, but here it means to measure depth. 'Leak' is slang for urinating.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that deepens becomes harder to sound or fathom, as plumbing a depth means measuring it.

clue.text: Request space to get nipple pierced by hand

parts.note: an en is a printer's space, half an em

indicators.note: something pierced has another thing driven into it, so the second item sits inside the first

parts.note: a teat is a nipple
R stands for right, as in right hand

explanation.surface: Someone asks for room to have a nipple piercing done by hand.
explanation.walkthrough: An en is a typesetting space; R for 'hand' comes from right hand, as in stage directions.
explanation.definitionFit: To entreat is to ask earnestly or beg, so it serves as a verb for request.
